body.text: Dr. Ikboljon Qoraboyev, an Uzbek international relations professor detained earlier this year in Kazakhstan, has reportedly been sentenced to 10 years in prison on espionage charges after a closed-door trial.

Ironically, news of the verdict arrived the same day that Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev delivered remarks at the 3rd Forum of Strategic Partners in Science and Higher Education in Astana. He set as a “strategic goal” the transformation of Kazakhstan into “an academic hub for Central Asia.” He aired ambitions to attract 100,000 international students to the country by 2029 and noted that “leading” higher education institutions from 11 countries had opened branches in Kazakhstan.
Tokayev also highlighted the more than 600 international professors who work at universities in Kazakhstan.

Qoraboyev, a well-known professor at Maksut Narikbayev University in Astana, was detained in early July. Reports of his arrest surfaced only in late August. Originally from Andijan, Uzbekistan, Qoraboyev’s detention has been shrouded in mystery, with neither Kazakh nor Uzbek officials commenting on the case.

Qoraboyev’s relatives, speaking to Azattyk Asia, said that he had been charge with espionage under Article 176 of Kazakhstan’s Criminal Code. Article 176 defines espionage as the collection, theft, or storage of “state secrets” by a foreign national for the purpose of transfer to a foreign state, or an international or foreign organization “for use against the national interests of the Republic of Kazakhstan.” Conviction carries a prison sentence of 10 to 15 years.

It is not known what specific actions on the part of Qoraboyev that Kazakh authorities deemed to be “collection, theft, or storage of ‘state secrets,’” why and how he would have access to “state secrets,” or which state he is alleged to have collected such material for.
Qoraboyev’s colleagues have stressed that his work was based on publicly available information.

When news of Qoraboyev’s detention broke in late August, a chill rippled through Kazakhstan’s academic sector. At the time, The Diplomat spoke with two Kazakhstan-based scholars about Qoraboyev’s arrest on condition of anonymity as both feared repercussions for speaking to the media. We referred to them as Amina and Bekzod:
Amina’s research overlaps with that of Qoraboyev. They heard about the arrest through a group chat on August 27 and met to discuss with other scholars that evening.

“The first reaction was horror; the initial announcement only included that a professor who worked on critical minerals had been arrested,” Amina said. “This was particularly concerning for those of us who work in this area and were concerned about our research.”
Amina noted that colleagues with upcoming trips to Uzbekistan scheduled were considering cancelling.
“We were discussing how this would affect regionalism in academia. Will academics be afraid to work together?” the scholar remarked.
The lack of information about Qoraboyev’s case, and his present status, perpetuates a sense of uncertainty.
Bekzod said the news came as “a surprise and shock as Ikboljon didn’t have access to state secrets.”

“If he is accused on the basis of compiling publicly available materials and then publishing or sending them for a review, this puts many local and international scholars at risk of similar accusations and creates an atmosphere of fear,” Bekzod argued.

In the months since that report, The Diplomat has been contacted by a handful of foreign academics asking whether it was safe for them to travel to Kazakhstan. Several Kazakhstan-based scholars have also told The Diplomat that they are receiving similar inquiries.

Qoraboyev’s case calls up that of Konstantin Syroezhkin, who was charged and convicted of treason in 2019. Syroezhkin was a noted Kazakhstani Sinologist and chief research officer at the Kazakhstan Institute for Strategic Studies. Like Qoraboyev, news of his arrest came to light months after it had occurred. He was convicted under Article 175 of the Kazakh criminal code – treason rather than espionage – and sentenced to 10 years in prison after a closed trial.
In 2024, Tokayev – himself a Sinologist – pardoned Syroezhkin.

Qoraboyev’s relatives told Azattyk Asia that they intend to seek a review of the case on appeal. They have called on Kazakh authorities to release materials related to the case, as well as for his full acquittal, reinstatement to his university position, recognition of possible violations against him, and the restoration of his reputation.

In his speech on November 19, Tokayev said that in the face of global competition for talent and technology, “Kazakhstan has made a clear strategic choice in favor of human capital. Above all, this means we value talent – both those cultivated in our country and those coming to us from abroad.”
Qoraboyev’s case suggests otherwise.
